h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving

Skander Moalla Affiliation: FAIR at Meta Affiliation: EPFL Work done at Meta    Ahmad Rammal Affiliation: FAIR at Meta Affiliation: CERMICS, ENPC, Institut Polytechnique de Paris    Niket Patel Affiliation: FAIR at Meta Affiliation: New York University Work done at Meta    Rémi Munos Affiliation: FAIR at Meta    Julia Kempe Affiliation: FAIR at Meta Affiliation: New York University Work done at Meta
Abstract

While progress in informal mathematics has come largely from scaling the chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning of frontier language models, formal theorem proving has increasingly relied on human-designed workflows around these models, such as planning, decomposition, and orchestrating specialized provers. This raises a bitter-lesson question: can a simple agentic loop that scales test-time compute match these workflows? The answer matters as formal verification must scale to keep up with frontier models producing research mathematics, yet new workflows rarely settle it, as their gains are often confounded with stronger models or more compute. We study this question with h1, a simple harness that gives a model an efficient interface to Lean 4 and keeps it working through verifier feedback and self-reflection, without imposing a decomposition or search structure. h1 reaches state-of-the-art results on PutnamBench, FATE-X, and FormalConjectures100-Solved, settles eight open problems in FormalConjectures, and, at matched models, matches or outperforms specialized workflows such as Goedel-Architect and AlphaProof Nexus, surprisingly showing that a single attempt (pass@1) can often scale to solve open problems. Through ablations and matched-model comparisons with Claude Code and AxProverBase, we find that simplicity alone is not enough: an efficient Lean interface largely determines cost and solve rate. We thus recommend that future work evaluate frontier models with efficient execution feedback before prescribing workflows, at the risk of bitter lessons.

††date: October 25, 2026††correspondence: Skander Moalla at skander.moalla@epfl.ch

1 Introduction

The bitter lesson predicts that general methods which scale with computation ultimately outperform approaches built around human domain knowledge (Sutton, 2019). However, while progress in informal mathematics has come from scaling frontier models’ chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning (OpenAI, 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Shang et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025), progress in formal proving has increasingly relied on human-designed workflows around those models. Indeed, formal proof assistants such as Lean (Moura and Ullrich, 2021) express mathematical statements and proofs in a precise language that can be checked mechanically. This includes intermediate proof steps, which naturally supports structured search that can be encoded as part of a workflow in a harness: the tools, context, and control loop around a model. Recent formal proving harnesses exploit this structure by orchestrating specialized provers or prescribing planning, decomposition, and proof refinement (Varambally et al., 2026; Chung et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Isenbaev and Hanin, 2026; Math Inc., 2026b). Only very recently has interest grown in simple loops that use the harness only to provide Lean feedback and sustain work (Requena et al., 2026; Tsoukalas et al., 2026; Humanfia, 2026; Kabra et al., 2026).

Formal mathematics thus raises a bitter-lesson question for harness design: with frontier models already capable of reasoning and agentic test-time scaling, can a simple test-time scaling loop match specialized workflows? And what should a simple harness provide to make that scaling effective and efficient? Do these simple methods offer better performance for the same cost? These questions matter increasingly as frontier models generate research mathematics whose informal arguments are difficult to verify. Indeed, scaling automated theorem proving (ATP) to produce mechanically checked proofs has become a necessary component of automated discovery (Tsoukalas et al., 2026; OpenAI, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026a; Patel et al., 2026). Yet new workflows are often presented alongside stronger models and more compute, or compared to baselines that scale poorly. This leaves unclear whether their gains hold against an efficient simple loop given enough test-time compute.

We tackle these questions with h1, a simple harness with an efficient interface to Lean 4 that imposes no decomposition or search structure. This loop keeps a model working until success or a cost cap stops it by iterating between a multi-turn block of reasoning and tool-calling, submission to a formal validator, and a reflection that compacts the transcript into a new context for the next iteration. Each additional iteration is akin to appending “Wait” to a model’s thinking in s1 (Muennighoff et al., 2025), extending the computation available at test time. We evaluate cost–success curves across benchmarks and open problems, accounting for inference cost and matching models where possible. Our findings are threefold:

  • •

    A bitter lesson for specialized harnesses: simple test-time scaling reaches frontier results without prescribed workflows (Sections 3.1 and 3.2). A simple loop often matches or Pareto-dominates specialized systems at matched models and comparable budgets, while reaching state-of-the-art results on PutnamBench (Tsoukalas et al., 2024), FATE-X (Jiang et al., 2026), and FormalConjectures100-Solved (Firsching et al., 2026) and settling eight open Formal Conjectures problems, and variants of Erdős 138 (Bloom, 2026a) and 337 (Bloom, 2026b). At matched models, h1 surpasses Goedel-Architect (Chung et al., 2026) at lower estimated cost; on five open Erdős problems, it Pareto-dominates full AlphaProof Nexus (APN) (Tsoukalas et al., 2026) with the same LLM.

  • •

    Longer attempts can be more efficient than repetition (Section 3.3). With sequential test-time scaling, pass@1 traces a budget-dependent curve that can Pareto-dominate pass@kk: on five Erdős problems, extending h1 can cost less than repeating h1 or APN basic (Tsoukalas et al., 2026).

  • •

    A simple harness still needs efficient interaction, reliable feedback, and sustained progress (Section 4). Among simple loops, harness design produces large differences in solve rates and cost. Controlled ablations and comparisons with AxProverBase (Requena et al., 2026), Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026a), and Humanfia (Humanfia, 2026) show the value of a reliable and efficient interface to Lean with search tools, a loop that sustains repair and reflection, and efficient reasoning and cache reuse.

Our results show that a simple harness can match or outperform more complex systems, extending the bitter lesson to harness design in ATP and plausibly other structured environments. Frontier models keep improving their reasoning and adaptation to execution feedback, and harnesses should help these capabilities scale through efficient interaction with the environment rather than impose workflows. Future work should thus evaluate frontier models with efficient execution feedback before prescribing workflows, or risk a bitter lesson.

2 Methods

We first introduce the formal-proving task, benchmarks, and baselines, and explain how we evaluate test-time scaling. We then describe h1’s tools and interaction loop, which let the model work efficiently and sustain progress as its inference budget grows.

2.1 Experimental setup

Formal proving.

In Lean (Moura and Ullrich, 2021), a formal statement specifies a mathematical claim and its assumptions; the agent must complete its proof in a source file. Mathlib (The mathlib Community, 2020) is a shared library of formalized mathematics that provides definitions and previously proved results. Compiling the file checks the proof and returns errors. During proof development, open goals list what remains to be proved. Additionally, formal validation tools such as SafeVerify (GasStationManager, 2024) allow checking the final proof against the original statement, rejecting placeholders for unfinished steps and added assumptions.

Benchmarks.

We evaluate on formal statements of increasing difficulty. PutnamBench (Tsoukalas et al., 2024) contains 672 problems from the past Putnam undergraduate competitions; for controlled comparisons, we use Putnam100, the same 100-problem subset used by AxProverBase (Requena et al., 2026). We also use the 12 problems of the 2025 Putnam competition, formalized both in PutnamBench and by Numina (Liu et al., 2026b). IMO 2026 contains the 6 problems of the 2026 International Mathematical Olympiad, the leading competition for high-school students, as formalized by Axiom (Axiom Math, 2026a). FATE-X (Jiang et al., 2026) contains 100 algebra problems at PhD qualifying-exam level or beyond, and FormalQualBench (Math Inc., 2026a) 23 theorems at PhD qualifying-exam level. Formal Conjectures (Firsching et al., 2026) collects formalized research conjectures; we evaluate on FC100-solved, a random sample of 100 problems with known informal solutions, and on open targets. Appendix C.1 records benchmark source revisions and Lean/Mathlib versions. We omit older benchmarks such as miniF2F (Zheng et al., 2022), which modern models essentially saturate. PutnamBench mainly tests efficiency, while FATE-X, FormalQualBench, and FC100-solved remain unsaturated at our scale. Putnam 2025 and IMO 2026 are recent enough to be unseen by the models released before them (Appendix E.10). Open conjectures, such as those in Formal Conjectures (Firsching et al., 2026), test progress beyond problems with known solutions.

Models and baselines.

We evaluate frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, alongside open-weight DeepSeek V4 Flash (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026) and Leanstral 1.5 (Kabra et al., 2026). We select baselines representing the most competitive results on our benchmarks as of August 27, 2026, alongside simple loops that help isolate the contribution of harness design. All state-of-the-art (SOTA) claims use this comparison cutoff (Appendix C.2). To compare with human-designed workflows, we include systems that enforce planning, decomposition, or agent roles in code: Goedel-Architect (Chung et al., 2026), MerLean (Li et al., 2026a), and full AlphaProof Nexus (Tsoukalas et al., 2026). OpenGauss (Math Inc., 2026b) instead prescribes a plan–review workflow to a general coding agent through instruction files (skills), while Numina (Liu et al., 2026b) gives a general coding agent optional tools that consult a natural-language (informal) prover and other models, and prescribes a subagent workflow for its hardest problem. Comparisons with other simple loops test interaction efficiency and persistence; these include Humanfia (Humanfia, 2026), APN basic (Tsoukalas et al., 2026) (AlphaProof Nexus’s single-agent loop), and our same-model reruns of both AxProverBase (Requena et al., 2026) and Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026a). We also report the published scores of trained provers, such as Seed-Prover 1.5 (Chen et al., 2025a), where they still define the SOTA. Appendix A discusses additional related work.

Measuring test-time scaling with cost per task.

Prior work very rarely compares systems at matched inference compute. Earlier theorem-proving work focused on training better models, with evaluation emphasizing solve rates rather than inference cost. As improvements increasingly come from inference-time search, repair, and orchestration, these reporting conventions have persisted even as an attempt has come to mean very different amounts of computation. For example, on PutnamBench, one Goedel-Architect attempt permits up to 16 revisions of its proof plan (Chung et al., 2026), while one AxProverBase attempt permits 50 agent iterations (Requena et al., 2026). Both papers report these as pass@1, but matching attempt counts do not match inference budgets; Appendix C.4 gives further examples. Even with the same model, output tokens can cost up to 100×100\times as much as cached input (Table 9). As inference-time methods drive more of the progress, accounting for their cost should become standard practice. We compare inference cost, holding the model fixed to compare harnesses or the harness fixed to measure model progress. Throughout the paper, dollar amounts for our experiments denote API-equivalent costs computed from recorded token usage and the rates in Table 9. At budget $BB per problem, solve count includes problems with a verified proof within budget. Average cost includes all problems, including failures, with each problem’s cost capped at $BB.

2.2 h1: a simple harness for efficient test-time scaling

h1 keeps a model working on a Lean proof until an external validator accepts it or the budget runs out (Figure 2). In each iteration, the model reasons and calls tools in a ReAct loop (Yao et al., 2023) for at most TT turns, editing a persistent working file; every edit is compiled and returns errors and open goals. The iteration ends when the model submits the file, which an external validator then checks against the original statement, also accepting checked disproofs where supported (Appendix C.2). If the validator rejects the submission, a reflection LLM compacts the transcript and feedback into verified progress, lessons from failed attempts, and useful lemma names, and discourages giving up, as in Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023), and AxProverBase (Requena et al., 2026); the model then continues from the current file with this summary. The loop builds on APN basic (Tsoukalas et al., 2026), AxProverBase, and the Ralph loop from software engineering (Huntley, 2025; Macedo, 2026).

A simple loop with an efficient interface.

h1 imposes no decomposition, planning, or search structure. Instead, it gives the model an efficient interface to Lean, with targeted edits rather than rewritten proofs, immediate compiler feedback, and a context that grows and is cached within an iteration. Optional tools let the model search Mathlib, inspect definitions, and test proof fragments, and the model decides which to use and how to develop the proof. Section 4 shows that these choices matter for both cost and success, and Appendix B details tools and prompts.

3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results

We first show that frontier models in h1 reach state-of-the-art results across competition and research mathematics. We then show that simple scaling often matches or outperforms specialized workflows at matched models and comparable inference costs, and that, even on open research problems, extending a single attempt can be more efficient than repetition.

3.1 A frontier model in a simple harness achieves state-of-the-art results

State-of-the-art results on established benchmarks.

With GPT-5.6 Sol, h1 achieves state-of-the-art results: 90/100 on FATE-X, 78/100 on FC100-solved, 14/23 on FormalQualBench, and all six IMO 2026 problems (Figure 3; Table 2). On PutnamBench, h1 with GPT-5.5 solves 670 of 672 problems. All these results use a single run per problem, without repetition or parallelism. Reaching state-of-the-art performance with a recent frontier model required only a larger inference budget, as the model keeps iterating, adjusting proofs and changing approaches without a prescribed workflow. Across our runs, individual accepted attempts reached up to 1,123 rounds of reflection (compaction), 95 active hours, or 7,124 lines of proof (Appendix G). An inexpensive open-weight model also surpasses specialized provers: DeepSeek V4 Flash in h1 solves 43 FATE-X problems at a $14.35 per-problem cap, exceeding Leanstral 1.5’s published 34 (Kabra et al., 2026). On FC100-solved, it matches the 50 solves (Firsching et al., 2026) of AlphaProof (Hubert et al., 2026) below an estimated $0.30 cap and reaches 64 at $4.89 per problem, close to the DM prover agent’s 66 (Google DeepMind, 2026). With Gemini 3.1 Pro, h1 also surpasses the DM prover agent on FC100-solved: it matches the agent’s 66 solves at a $25 rather than $100 cap per problem, then reaches 73 at $150 (Google DeepMind, 2026; Firsching et al., 2026).11 1 The DM prover agent’s model is not named; we infer Gemini 3.1 Pro from its apparent connection to AlphaProof Nexus (Tsoukalas et al., 2026). In line with the bitter lesson, the gains frontier models draw from scaling training compute carry over to an unchanged simple loop: in h1, GPT-5.6 Sol matches the DM prover agent’s 66 FC100-solved solves below a $9 cap, against $25 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and reaches 90 FATE-X solves at $38 per problem, against 81 at $113 (Figure 3).

Solving open problems and exposing misformalizations.

Beyond the solved subset of Formal Conjectures and benchmarks with possibly known informal solutions, we ran our system on 236 targets selected as open from Formal Conjectures (Appendix D). It settled eight of them (Table 1): variants of Erdős 138 and 337, three OEIS conjectures (A108081, A211417, A022030), the existence of an AME(9,10)(9,10) state (Open Quantum Problem 35), and two conjectures of Written on the Wall II. We document concisely the newly proven theorems in Appendix D, and our pull-request marking these as solved22 2 https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/6008/. Equally important as finding these proofs was our system’s ability to find misformalizations in Formal Conjectures: formal statements that do not express the intended conjecture. Our system found several by producing short disproofs of the written statement, for instance for the Poincaré conjecture, whose formalization was missing a hypothesis. Appendix D.2 lists all misformalizations found, most of which have since been fixed upstream.

These results establish the capability of a simple harness, and we show in the next section that simple scaling often matches specialized workflows with the same model and comparable inference cost.

3.2 The bitter lesson for specialized workflows

We show that, at matched models, simple test-time scaling recovers much of the performance of specialized workflows, often at lower inference cost, and that repetition (pass@kk) or a newer frontier model in the same loop usually closes any remaining gap (Figure 1; Table 2).

Simple test-time scaling can match specialized systems at lower cost.

On PutnamBench, one extended h1 attempt surpasses Goedel-Architect’s blueprint-based search, which assigns separate agents to prove the lemmas in a dependency graph. With the same DeepSeek V4 Flash model, h1 first matches its pass@1 score at comparable cost, then reaches 598 solves against 597 at pass@4 with informal proof seeding, at an estimated $1.08 versus $1.47 per problem (Chung et al., 2026) (Figure 1, left). Goedel-Architect’s tool-integrated reasoning baseline reaches only 54.5% at pass@32 on a 200-problem subset, compared with h1’s 89.0% at pass@1 on the full benchmark with the same model. With Gemini 3.1 Pro alone, h1 also matches Goedel-Architect’s July leaderboard result of 642 solves, which pairs Gemini 3.1 Pro with the cheaper DeepSeek V4 Pro, at a similar cost ($6.32 versus $5.80 per problem). The much stronger performance of a simple harness with the same model illustrates how a weak simple baseline can overstate the need for specialized workflows (Figure 6).

A simple loop solves the problem that needed a hand-designed workflow.

A single model in h1 also recovers the result of Numina-Lean-Agent, which reserved a specialized workflow for the hardest problem of Putnam 2025. Numina runs Opus 4.5 in Claude Code, a general coding agent, with optional tools that call other models: an informal prover built as a Gemini 3 Pro generator–verifier loop, and a discussion partner (Liu et al., 2026b). For that problem, A5, the authors switch to a coordinator that delegates blueprint decomposition, sketching, and proving to subagents, seeded with a GPT-5.2 hint and a $1,000 budget. On the same statements, GPT-5.2 alone solves all twelve in h1, including A5, in a single run per problem and without such a workflow, spending $81.52 on A5 against Numina’s $1,000 budget (Table 2). Also note that with Opus 4.5 alone, h1 solves seven problems against four for Numina without its informal prover, consistent with our finding that Claude Code, on which Numina builds, scales less effectively than h1 with the same model (Section 4).

Repetition closes most remaining gaps.

When a single h1 run falls short, rerunning the unsolved problems from a fresh context (residual pass@kk) closes most remaining gaps. Like h1 itself, repetition prescribes no workflow; it simply adds independent attempts, though often at a higher cost than extending a single run (Section 3.3). As long as that cost is counted, including failed attempts, repetition therefore belongs to the simple baseline against which specialized workflows should be tested. On Putnam 2025, h1 with Opus 4.7 solves eleven against MerLean’s twelve; retrying the remaining problem recovers all twelve within six attempts. On full PutnamBench, extra attempts on the last two problems let h1 with GPT-5.5 match Aleph Prover’s (Logical Intelligence, 2026) final 672/672 coverage at an estimated $17.86 versus about $74 per problem, counting the cost of failed attempts (Appendix C.4). On FormalQualBench (Math Inc., 2026a), OpenGauss (Math Inc., 2026b) instructs Claude Code to cycle through planning, proving, review, and replanning, generating several candidate proofs per open goal and extracting helper lemmas when a goal is stuck. The best of four h1 runs with Opus 4.6 matches its eight solves under the same four-hour limit. On these benchmarks, the only remaining exception after scaling and repetition is MerLean on FormalQualBench with Opus 4.7, which retains a one-problem advantage with or without the four-hour cutoff (Appendix E.1).

The next frontier model closes the rest.

In some rare cases, such as on FormalQualBench with MerLean (Li et al., 2026a), we find that repetition does not close the gap between h1 and the other methods. However, even in this case, replacing Opus 4.7 with its direct successor, Opus 4.8, is enough for h1 to overtake MerLean, with 13 against 10 solves at $49.46 rather than $118.35 per solve, and with GPT-5.6 Sol, h1 also solves the one problem that only MerLean had proved (Table 2). MerLean would likely also improve with Opus 4.8 or GPT-5.6 Sol, but we expect this gap to keep shrinking as newer models internalize the strategies that workflows prescribe. We see this as the bitter lesson at work, as newer models convert more training compute into capabilities that an unchanged simple loop directly benefits from.

3.3 Persisting can beat repetition, even on open problems

When an attempt can keep going, pass@1 is no longer a single number but a curve that grows with budget: within one run, the model can abandon an approach and try another. The question becomes whether spending more on one attempt beats spending the same on several. AlphaProof Nexus (APN) (Tsoukalas et al., 2026) found that its basic agent, a simple loop like h1, can Pareto-dominate its full system, which evolves proof sketches with LLM raters, parallel provers, and AlphaProof, but only through repetition: at pass@kk for large enough kk. APN reports each pass@kk, including pass@1, as a single point at a fixed budget, leaving open whether a single attempt given more budget can do what repetition does.

We evaluate h1 on the six open Erdős problems that APN reports individually, using the same model, Gemini 3.1 Pro. Following APN, we report mean cost conditional on success, charging each group its members’ summed cost up to the first accepted proof. This metric is undefined for a problem with no successful attempts, so Figure 1 (middle) compares the five problems that all three systems solve at least once. For h1, we show how pass@1 changes as the budget grows, rather than reporting a single point. As the budget grows, it matches APN basic’s pass@1 at lower cost, then exceeds both APN basic’s pass@3 (75.4% at $191) and full APN (76% at $317), reaching 82.5% at $121. On these five problems, giving one h1 attempt more time achieves a higher solve rate at lower cost than three attempts of APN basic. Full APN retains an advantage over both APN basic and h1 on the remaining problem, Erdős 125, where all sixteen h1 attempts end in Lean timeouts (Appendix E.6).

APN’s conditional metric gives a first view of this depth–breadth trade-off, but omits spending on groups with no accepted proof (Appendix E.6). To account for these costs and separate compute allocation and isolate differences between harnesses, we also compare longer attempts with repetition within h1, using mean spend across all successful and failed groups (Figure 12). On the same five problems, pass@1 reaches 82.5% at $138 in mean spend including failures, whereas pass@3 needs $202 to reach at least that rate. Thus, the advantage of longer attempts at these budgets persists when failed searches are charged. Repetition reaches higher success rates at larger budgets. The right balance between depth (longer attempts) and breadth (more attempts) therefore depends on the budget and problem and is hard to set in advance. The bitter lesson suggests leaving this choice to the model rather than to hand-set budgets.

4 What a harness must provide for efficient test-time scaling

Leaving the proof workflow to the model does not make the harness irrelevant: with the same model, simple loops differ several-fold in solve rate and cost. We explain these differences, and what makes h1 a state-of-the-art harness and an effective Lean baseline, by pairing comparisons with other simple loops with ablations on h1 that vary its tools, prompts, reflection, turns between reflections, and reasoning effort. The resulting lessons concern the interface, persistence, and context management, and should transfer beyond the automated theorem proving domain, to agents that work against a verifier in rich environments allowing structured development and retrieval, such as software verification and coding in large libraries and codebases.

An efficient, reliable interface lets the model act in small steps and look things up.

In h1, the model edits a persistent working file over many turns, sees compiler feedback after every edit, and can search the library or test a proof fragment at any point. AxProverBase (Requena et al., 2026) instead makes one round of tool calls, then regenerates a complete proof after each round of feedback. With the same Gemini 3 Flash model and a $20 budget, it solves 18 Putnam100 problems against h1’s 69, and trails in all six settings we compare (Figure , left). A reliable interface also removes avoidable failures by construction: 42.2% of AxProverBase’s failed compilations stop at an invalid library import, which cannot occur in h1 because its file already imports all of Mathlib (Figure 19). Likewise, h1 retries transient API failures and restores the file after a Lean timeout, whereas some Claude Code runs failed through API errors and repeated timeouts even after restarts (Appendix E.9). Library search, which AxProverBase found the least useful of its components, matters much more when the model can act on its results over many turns: without search tools, the REPL, or the language server, h1 solves 49 Putnam100 and 49 FATE-X problems, against 69 and 63 with all tools (Figure 21). Any single search tool or the REPL recovers most of this gain, and removing any one tool from the full set costs at most four solves: what matters is the ability to look up and check, not a particular tool. Other simple loops with less efficient interfaces reach h1’s solve rates only at higher cost. APN basic (Tsoukalas et al., 2026) lacks dedicated search tools; on the five-problem Erdős subset, extending a single h1 attempt can be more efficient than repeating APN basic (Section 3.3). Humanfia (Humanfia, 2026) checks proofs only through shell commands and restarts its coding agent in a fresh session each round, carrying over only the proof file and reviewer feedback; with GPT-5.5, it spends five times more than h1 for the same 670 PutnamBench solves. A harness should thus support the model by offering a persistent workspace edited in small steps, immediate feedback, ways to retrieve and check what the model needs, and robust handling of predictable failures, leaving their use to the model.

The loop, not the model, decides when to stop.

Test-time compute helps only if the harness turns a larger budget into continued work. With Opus 4.8, native Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026a) solves 63 FATE-X problems; giving it our prompt and our Lean tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), in place of its built-in shell and file tools, raises this to 73, while h1 reaches 83 (Figure , right; 81, 95, and 99 on Putnam100). Access to verification helps, but the model can still stop without calling the validator or give up after a rejection; in h1, a rejection starts another iteration with the working file, the feedback, and a reflection summary (Appendix E.9). Within h1, the system prompts matter most on open problems. Unlike one-line prompts, our detailed prompts describe the tools, set rules for statement integrity and disproofs, and tell the prover not to give up because a problem is open and the reflection LLM not to endorse such a decision (Appendix B.2). On six Erdős problems, a single attempt with them outperforms six attempts with one-line prompts at the same $150 cap per attempt (Figure 4, left). Reflection, which carries verified progress and lessons into the next iteration, raises h1 with DeepSeek V4 Flash from 554 to 598 PutnamBench solves, consistent with AxProverBase’s findings (Figure 6). None of these tells the model how to prove: the harness decides whether the model keeps going, not how.

Reuse context, reset it before it degrades, and think more per turn.

Each turn in a continuing context rereads it from cache, typically ten times cheaper than uncached input and a hundred times cheaper than output, whereas each restart discards it. AxProverBase sits at one extreme: output accounts for 89% of its $17.39 per problem, against 34% of h1’s $9.00, and it reuses at most 0.5% of its input from cache, against 74–94% for h1 (Figure 17). Varying the number of turns between reflections in h1 exposes the same trade-off (Figure 4, right). With one turn, h1 solves 50 Putnam100 and 39 FATE-X problems, against 72 and 65 with ten turns, and pays roughly twice as much per solve. With 200 turns instead of one, the cached share of input rises from 0.2% to 86%, yet solves drop to 60 and 52 (Figure 28): caching makes long contexts cheap but not productive, consistent with context rot (Hong et al., 2025). Thinking more per turn is a better use of budget. AxProverBase found that raising the thinking budget from 10k to 32k tokens gains as much as doubling the number of iterations, at lower cost. In h1, higher reasoning effort solves more at lower total cost: with Gemini 3.1 Pro, it solves 89 Putnam100 problems at $20.63 each with low effort and 99 at $5.34 with high effort, needing far fewer compilations (Figure 27). In short, a harness for long-horizon agents should let the model work in one context long enough to reuse it, compact that context before it degrades, and favor reasoning over repeated failed attempts.

5 Conclusion, limitations, and discussion

Conclusion.

We asked whether harnesses for frontier models should prescribe hand-designed workflows or give the model a simple loop and a larger budget. With h1, a simple loop with an efficient interface to Lean, test-time compute alone reaches state-of-the-art results and matches or surpasses hand-designed workflows at the same model and comparable cost. We find that a single longer attempt in this loop can even outperform repetition on open problems. Getting the details of the harness right still matters: its interface, persistence, and context management determine how efficiently compute turns into progress. Before designing a workflow, one should thus carefully try a frontier model in a simple loop at a realistic budget.

Limitations and discussion.

We acknowledge that most frontier models are black boxes, and that we cannot measure the extent to which benchmark exposure during training could narrow the gap between specialized workflows and a simple loop, but where possible we used models that predate the problems or their solutions, such as Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.2 for Putnam 2025 and GPT-5.6 Sol for IMO 2026 (Appendix E.10). Across the 707 benchmark problems on which we compare the simple loop with a specialized workflow, we find only two exceptions where the specialized harness is able to solve a problem we are not33 3 Full APN solves Erdős 125, where all sixteen h1 attempts end in Lean timeouts, and MerLean with Opus 4.7 proves BurnsidePrimeDegree, which h1 with Opus 4.8 does not prove in our run, although h1 with GPT-5.6 Sol does (Appendix E.1)..

Regarding scale, h1 works on a single file, whereas formalizations that exceed a context window, such as those of Fermat’s Last Theorem (Anthropic, 2026b) or entire textbooks (Rammal et al., 2026), require dependency management across files, and codebase-level validation, as well as parallel agents that share intermediate results to complete the task in reasonable time: in OpenAI’s Navier–Stokes resolution, about 10,000 agents exchanged millions of messages over 88 hours (OpenAI, 2026a). Our tools also cover only Lean, not numerical computation, simulation, visualization, or web search. What makes a simple loop efficient and effective at that scale is the natural next question. Following the bitter lesson, parallel agents, codebase management, and richer tools should be added without prescribing their use, for instance by letting agents communicate freely rather than through a fixed hierarchy.

h1’s interface and tools are themselves hand-designed, which the bitter lesson might discourage. Yet human design and leveraging computation need not run counter to each other (Sutton, 2019); the question is where each helps most first. In formal mathematics, spending compute on the reasoning of frontier models, and using human effort on the interface currently works best. Further ahead, a model could build and deploy its own harness for a problem and become more efficient than the human-designed interfaces.

Appendix A Related Work

Trained provers.

Neural provers began with tactic prediction inside proof search (Polu and Sutskever, 2020; Lample et al., 2022; Polu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023; Kumarappan et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025; George et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025a; Xin et al., 2025b), reaching olympiad level with AlphaProof’s reinforcement learning and search (Hubert et al., 2026). Later models generate whole proofs (First et al., 2023; Xin et al., 2025a; Ren et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Dong and Ma, 2025; Lin et al., 2025b; Lin et al., 2026) or are trained for agentic, tool-integrated proving (Chen et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026). These systems contribute trained models rather than a harness around a given model, so we compare against their reported scores where available (Section 3.1).

Harnesses around generalist models.

Following informal-to-formal sketching (Jiang et al., 2023) and early agentic loops (Thakur et al., 2024; Ospanov et al., 2025), recent systems add proof-specific structure around generalist models: auxiliary lemmas and informal reasoners (Baba et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a), multi-agent proving (Breen et al., 2026), recursive decomposition (Zhou et al., 2025; Varambally et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a), blueprints (Chung et al., 2026), optional informal-prover and multi-model tools (Liu et al., 2026b), and evolutionary search over proof sketches in full APN (Tsoukalas et al., 2026); Seed-Prover (Chen et al., 2025b) and Aristotle (Achim et al., 2025) build such structure around their own trained provers. We compare with several of these using the same model (Section 3.2). Rögnvaldsson et al. (2026) reduce the compute such workflows spend on failed attempts with a learned controller; we instead remove the workflow. Among simple loops, we compare with AxProverBase (Requena et al., 2026), Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026a; Math Inc., 2026a), Humanfia’s loop with reviewer feedback (Humanfia, 2026), and APN basic (Tsoukalas et al., 2026) (Section 4). AxProverBase demonstrates the strength of minimal agents and self-reflection for retaining lessons (Requena et al., 2026). We extend this evidence to open problems and compare harnesses using the same models and accounting for inference cost. These agents use Lean interfaces including the REPL (leanprover-community, 2023), Pantograph (Aniva et al., 2025), the Kimina server (Santos et al., 2025), and lean-lsp-mcp (Dressler, 2025).

Autoformalization systems.

Aleph (Isenbaev and Hanin, 2026), AxiomProver (Axiom Math, 2025; Axiom Math, 2026a), and OpenGauss (Math Inc., 2026b) target formalization more broadly, as do efforts on major results (Anthropic, 2026b), corpora (Rammal et al., 2026), and research mathematics (Zhang et al., 2026; Moakhar et al., 2026). OpenGauss prescribes its planning and review workflow through skill instructions, whereas Goedel-Architect enforces its blueprint search in code. We compare with Aleph, AxiomProver, and OpenGauss only on proof completion for fixed statements, which evaluates part of what they do; our results say nothing about their value in open-ended formalization (Section 5).

Test-time scaling and simple loops.

Inference compute scales through repeated sampling (Brown et al., 2024; Snell et al., 2025) and longer reasoning (OpenAI, 2024; Guo et al., 2025); h1 extends s1’s budget forcing (Muennighoff et al., 2025) from one chain of thought to an agent’s iterations. For agents, test-time scaling has been studied in general (Zhu et al., 2025) and in coding (Kim et al., 2026; Ding and Zhang, 2026); Li et al. (2026b) find sequential scaling limited by context and parallel scaling by verification, the two limitations addressed by h1’s reflection and verifier. Rather than hand-crafting test-time scaling strategies, Zheng et al. (2026) have an agent discover them. h1 combines ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) with self-reflection (Shinn et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023), and enforces external validation, which LLMs need to self-correct (Huang et al., 2024; Kambhampati et al., 2024). In software engineering (Jimenez et al., 2024), interfaces matter (Yang et al., 2024), simple pipelines and minimal agents compete with complex ones (Xia et al., 2025; SWE-agent Team, 2025), and the Ralph loop runs an agent until verification succeeds (Huntley, 2025; Macedo, 2026). Following Kapoor et al. (2025), we evaluate accuracy jointly with cost (Section 2.1).

Benchmarks and validation.

Beyond earlier benchmarks (Zheng et al., 2022; Ying et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025; Ravi et al., 2026; Letson et al., 2026), we evaluate on PutnamBench (Tsoukalas et al., 2024), FATE (Jiang et al., 2026), FormalQualBench (Math Inc., 2026a), and Formal Conjectures (Firsching et al., 2026), accepting proofs through a formal validator (GasStationManager, 2024; Lean FRO, 2025; Axiom Math, 2026b) since compilation alone need not prove the intended statement.

Appendix B Tools, Prompts, and Error Handling in h1

This appendix specifies the tools, prompts, and error handling used by h1 (Section 2.2): tool interfaces (Table 3), prompt variants (Table 4), reflection safeguards (Table 5), and Lean failure handling (Table 6). Formal validation is described in Appendix C.2.

B.1 Tools

B.2 Prompts for proof search and reflection

h1 uses two LLM roles (Figure 2). The multi-turn LLM performs proof search by editing the working file and calling tools. After validation fails, the reflection LLM summarizes the attempt and verifier feedback into compacted context for the next iteration. The multi-turn LLM receives this context alongside the original statement, current working file, and verifier feedback. Our Detailed prompt is adapted from the prompts of AxProverBase (Requena et al., 2026) and APN basic (Tsoukalas et al., 2026). Table 4 compares the Brief and Detailed system prompts for the multi-turn LLM and the reflection LLM. Each LLM has these two prompt versions. The Detailed prompts are reproduced in the labeled boxes below.

Detailed prompt text.

The boxes reproduce both LLMs’ detailed system prompts with all tools enabled, adapting only Markdown formatting for print. Tool-specific sections are omitted when those tools are unavailable. Table 4 quotes both brief prompts; the split ablations exchange them. User messages insert the original statement, initial Lean feedback, current proof, latest attempt, and compacted context; the reflection LLM also receives the transcript, except with no_transcript.

B.3 Lean feedback and error handling

Lean errors and process failures receive different treatment (Table 6). A successful Lean restart lets the same proof attempt continue; it does not start a new independent model attempt. After a connection failure, h1 repeats the same Lean command without resampling the model response. Interrupted executions can resume from saved proof state within the same benchmark attempt; they are not additional samples for pass@kk.

A deterministic Lean failure that recurs on three consecutive executions is counted as an unsolved problem. Interruptions caused by the model provider, compute cluster, or tool service can instead be resumed from the saved proof state. Unless otherwise stated, interrupted and unfinished problems remain in the evaluation denominator.

Appendix C Proof Validation, Evaluation, and Cost Accounting

This appendix defines which proofs count as solutions, how inference costs and budget-limited solve rates are computed, and how uncertainty is estimated. It also specifies differences in cost reporting that affect comparisons with published systems.

C.1 Benchmark revisions and Lean environments

Table 7 summarizes the source revisions and Lean/Mathlib environments in the setup recipes for the benchmarks used in this paper. Putnam100 and the 2025 slice share the PutnamBench source; the separate Numina formalization is listed independently.

Formal Conjectures snapshot and open status.

The FC100-solved and Erdős/APN setups use Formal Conjectures revision 7862bf6a, dated April 29, 2026, with Lean/Mathlib 4.27.0. This source date is distinct from the May 6 benchmark release. We use the original solved subset, FC100Solved, subsequently renamed FC100SolvedSet1 upstream. The separate evaluation of 236 open targets is described in Appendix D.

C.2 Formal validation

A compiling file need not prove the intended theorem: it may contain sorry, change assumptions, or introduce axioms. We use SafeVerify (GasStationManager, 2024) to compare compiled submissions with an immutable challenge, check target declarations and permitted axioms, and replay new declarations through Lean’s kernel. Imported modules remain part of the trusted environment.

Comparator (Lean FRO, 2025) also checks statement agreement, permitted axioms, and kernel acceptance, and integrates sandboxed compilation of the challenge and submission. AXLE’s verify_proof tool (Axiom Math, 2026b) offers similar checks, including optional verification of a statement’s negation, through a hosted API. SafeVerify instead takes already-compiled .olean files, so the harness must isolate compilation and protect the challenge and imported dependencies (GasStationManager, 2024). We chose SafeVerify for its disproof support, which allows a fixed conjecture to be settled by proving it or its negation, and because Comparator’s Landlock/landrun sandbox was not supported in our execution environment. We built SafeVerify against each benchmark’s toolchain and implemented the isolated compilation procedure in Table 8.

Comparison cutoff.

We stopped adding results from other methods to our comparison set after August 27, 2026. All state-of-the-art claims in this paper are relative to results publicly available by that date; later work is discussed only as related or concurrent work. For PutnamBench, the leaderboard snapshot of August 27, 2026 includes Aleph’s and Humanfia’s 672-solve results and Goedel-Architect’s July update. Source access dates after the cutoff reflect checks made while writing, rather than an extension of the comparison period.

C.3 Inference budgets and cost curves

An attempt can denote a single model call, an iterative repair session, or a complete multi-stage pipeline. For example, Goedel-Architect allows up to 16 blueprint refinements within one PutnamBench attempt (Chung et al., 2026). Matching attempt counts therefore need not match inference cost. Total token counts are also insufficient: uncached input, cached input, and output have different costs, with output tokens costing up to 100×100\times as much as cached input in our price cards. Ideally, we would compare inference FLOPs directly, but closed-model providers rarely disclose the information needed to measure them. We therefore use inference cost as a practical proxy and compare cost with the model held fixed to assess harness differences; input, cached input, cache writes, and output are priced separately using the reference rates in Table 9, including applicable long-context rates. These API-equivalent costs quantify token usage under a specified price card, not actual expenditure.

For problem ii, let cic_{i} be its total API-equivalent cost and aia_{i} its cost at first acceptance, with ai=∞a_{i}=\infty if unsolved. At per-problem cap $BB, the solve count is ∑i𝟏[ai≤B]\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}[a_{i}\leq B]. Figures with a budget axis plot this count against $BB; figures with an average-cost axis plot it against 1n​∑imin⁡(ci,B)\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\min(c_{i},B). Where first-acceptance cost is unavailable, the final cost of a successful attempt is used as its proxy. Cost bars average all recorded problems, including failures. A nominal cap is an allocation limit; recorded final cost can exceed it when the last model call crosses the limit. Every curve ends at a finite budget. We stopped runs when further spending became unreasonable under our time and compute limits, or when Lean failed in ways the harness could not recover from, such as repeated REPL timeouts; the latter call for a better Lean interface rather than a different loop.

Matching prior work’s reporting conventions.

To compare with published results, we follow the corresponding benchmark’s reporting conventions where needed. In Table 2, costs are campaign totals for Putnam 2025, per-problem means for PutnamBench and IMO, and means over successful problems for FormalQualBench. Numina reports a budget cap rather than a cost derived from token usage. Putnam and IMO times are summed across problems; FormalQualBench times average successes, and Humanfia’s IMO time includes only API time. Putnam 2025 uses Numina’s statements, whereas the PutnamBench 2025 slice uses separate formalizations. Our FormalQualBench Opus 4.6 result is the best of four seeds (7, 6, 8, and 6 solves); the leaderboard model attribution to Opus 4.6 is inferred. The best@6 row on PutnamBench’s 2025 slice gives the order of magnitude a favourable seed can reach among six attempts; its cost counts successful attempts only. We report it next to pass@1 and pass@4, and the four FormalQualBench seeds individually, so that the spread is visible; we draw no conclusion from the best seed alone. The cost measure therefore changes across tables and figures: to compare with a published number, we adopt that work’s convention, such as campaign totals, budget caps, or cost conditional on success. Wherever our data allow, we also report the full cost including failed attempts, and we claim comparable or lower cost at matched models rather than uniform cost dominance across systems.

C.4 PutnamBench results and published cost conventions

Table 10 reports solve percentages so that benchmarks with different denominators can be distinguished. Published state-of-the-art results often combine several campaigns that re-attempt residual problems, such as Aleph’s budget re-launches (Logical Intelligence, 2026). Where possible, we report a single campaign without re-running residual problems; the one exception is the targeted completion of the last two problems described below. Published costs are not uniformly measured: Goedel-Architect reports campaign totals ($294 and $985.67, divided by 672 here), whereas Aleph’s first three points report cost per successful problem (Logical Intelligence, 2026). Aleph’s final result reports $73.98 per problem, excluding attempts preceding formalization fixes; the figure rounds this to $74. Humanfia reports cost per benchmark problem. Its current results attribute 672 solves at $44.50 to GPT-5.6 Sol; the earlier GPT-5.5 result is 670 at $44.60 (repository accessed 14 September 2026). Hilbert’s approximate $244 cost is an estimate attributed to Chung et al. (2026, Table 2), based on pass@1 statistics. It is not measured cost for the 70% headline result: Hilbert did not track compute for that multi-attempt run, and its separate compute-tracked pass@1 run achieved 55.9% (Varambally et al., 2026, Appendix A.6).

Targeted completion of the last two problems.

The GPT-5.5 continuation ran eight replicas each on putnam_2013_a5 and putnam_2021_a6 using benchmark revision b9e18f6 and Lean 4.27, obtaining seven and one SafeVerify-accepted proofs, respectively. PutnamBench has corrected formalizations since our original campaign, including that of putnam_2013_a5; these corrections also allowed other systems to reach 672 solves (Logical Intelligence, 2026; Humanfia, 2026). The 672 result therefore combines our original campaign with the corrected statements. For each problem ii, we estimate parallel stopping cost as ∑jmin⁡(ci​j,si)\sum_{j}\min(c_{ij},s_{i}), where ci​jc_{ij} is replica jj’s final cost and sis_{i} the cheapest successful replica’s cost. This adds $5,839.36, yielding $17.86 per problem across 672 problems. It assumes cancellation at equal dollar cost, not equal elapsed time. Including the full $7,938.75 continuation instead gives $20.99 per problem.

C.5 Estimated DeepSeek API costs

DeepSeek V4 Flash was served locally without recorded cache-hit counters. We reconstruct cache reuse from unchanged prompt prefixes in the traces, separately for each agent role and resetting at resume boundaries. This assumes that reusable prefixes remain cached. We price the recorded input and output tokens, including reflection and reasoning, at the fixed April 26 rates in Table 9. Goedel-Architect retains its reported costs; its price card and cache usage are unspecified. This gives 598/672 solves at an estimated $1.08 per problem, with 92.27% reconstructed cache reuse.

C.6 Statistical significance and uncertainty

Many comparisons in this paper rest on a single run per configuration. Repeating every run would multiply an already large inference cost, and we judge single runs sufficient for the claims they support, because most of them are existence claims: that a simple loop can reach a given score at a given cost. Since every accepted proof is formally verified, one run establishes such a claim; for example, a single run shows that h1 with GPT-5.5 can solve 670 of the 672 PutnamBench problems. Where a claim requires statistical significance, we repeat runs or resample problems and report 95% confidence intervals, as in the tool ablation (Figure 21), the Erdős prompt comparison (Figure 4), and the reflection-input costs (Table 16).

Ablation effect sizes.

Figure 21 summarizes both coverage and cost. Its tool comparison rewards solving earlier: if S⁡(b)S(b) is the fraction solved by cost bb, we summarize the curve by E⁡(B)=100B​∫0BS⁡(b)​𝑑bE(B)=\frac{100}{B}\int_{0}^{B}S(b)\,db. Equivalently, each problem solved at cost ai≤Ba_{i}\leq B earns 100​(1−ai/B)100(1-a_{i}/B) and an unsolved problem earns zero; the score averages all 100 problems. The API-equivalent cost of a successful run is our proxy for first-acceptance cost. We compare configurations by averaging their score differences on the same problems. Upper boxes use the working-file-only configuration with the detailed prompt as reference; lower boxes use all tools with the detailed prompt.

The 95% percentile intervals use 50,000 bootstrap resamples of whole paired problems, sharing resampling indices across configurations within a benchmark.

For the Erdős prompt comparison in Figure 4, we compute 95% bootstrap intervals by resampling the observed runs with replacement: 16 runs for the detailed-prompt reference and ten for each other configuration. Each sampled run retains its outcomes on all six problems. Each resample recomputes pass@kk at the $150 per-attempt cap, with crashes and missing results counted as unsolved.

C.7 Proof screening

We recover AxProverBase proofs from traces’ final candidates. Removing native_decide removes 35 accepted proofs across nine runs. Screened counts are used in the aggregate matched-cap comparison in Section 4; Figure 1 (right) retains unscreened counts. SafeVerify accepts our proofs and rejects sorryAx, new axioms, and evaluation via native_decide.

Appendix D Open-Problem Proofs and Statement Corrections

D.1 Statements proved

Table 12 states the eight mathematical results reported in Section 3.1 and identifies their Lean proof files. Written on the Wall II Conjectures 100 and 314 were proved after correcting their statements; the other six concern the named distributed targets. Each result concerns the specific variant and formal statement listed in the table.

D.2 Misformalizations and editable answers

Kernel checking establishes a proposition, but does not establish that it expresses the intended problem. Table 13 summarizes statement defects identified in our Formal Conjectures audit and the benchmark repairs. An editable answer creates a separate problem: when a submission can change a definition referenced by the target, it can make the target reflexive or vacuous. Such outputs do not count as solutions. We fix answers or quantify witnesses satisfying the intended mathematical constraints, and exclude exact-answer targets when that transformation would discard the mathematical question.

The smooth four-dimensional Poincaré variant illustrates a missing hypothesis. Its SmoothConjectureFor predicate omitted T2Space, allowing non-Hausdorff smooth manifolds homotopy equivalent to 𝕊4\mathbb{S}^{4} but not homeomorphic to it. A concurrent upstream correction adds the Hausdorff assumption and a Lean counterexample to the old statement (Deicyde, 2026).

Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3

This appendix reports the per-problem results, model comparisons, and analyses of failed attempts supporting Section 3.

E.1 Remaining advantages of specialized systems

Among 707 problems, two fixed-model exceptions stood out: the group-theoretic BurnsidePrimeDegree and the density problem Erdős 125 (Appendix E.4). On FormalQualBench with Opus 4.7, MerLean leads h1 by one solve with or without the four-hour cutoff (Table 2). MerLean proves BurnsidePrimeDegree in 3h12m with a 32-node decomposition (Li et al., 2026a); eleven h1 attempts fail despite a combined $6,000 and 255 hours. With Opus 4.8, we stopped our FormalQualBench run by hand after 17 hours because of time and compute limits (Appendix C.3); it had not proved BurnsidePrimeDegree by iteration 19 ($195), so that run’s 13/23 is a lower bound. With GPT-5.6 Sol, however, h1 proves BurnsidePrimeDegree (Table 2). On Erdős 125, full APN reaches 50% at pass@1, basic reaches only 10% at pass@10, and all sixteen h1 attempts end in unrecoverable Lean REPL timeouts, an interface limitation (Appendix C.3; Figure 8; Appendix E.4).

Specialized harnesses may still reduce time to a solution, even when h1 matches their solve rate at lower cost. Numina solves twelve in less summed time than h1 with GPT-5.2, possibly helped by faster constituent models (Table 2). Multi-agent parallelization could further reduce elapsed time, a capability orthogonal to h1’s simple sequential search that we discuss in Section 5.

E.2 PutnamBench: reflection and specialized provers

E.3 DeepSeek V4 Flash on FC100-solved and FATE-X

Because of a configuration error on our side, the DeepSeek V4 Flash runs on FC100-solved and FATE-X in Figure 3 ran with self-reflection disabled. Figure 7 reproduces both panels with this setting labelled. With the same model on PutnamBench, reflection substantially improves coverage (Figure 6), so these curves may understate h1 with DeepSeek V4 Flash. We will add runs with self-reflection in a subsequent version.

E.4 Erdős problems: individual scaling curves

E.5 Erdős problems: prompt and model ablations

E.6 Comparing success and cost with AlphaProof Nexus

We selected the six Erdős problem instances in Figure 3 of Tsoukalas et al. (2026) for direct comparison: 12(i), 12(ii), 26, 125, 138, and 152.

AlphaProof Nexus operates on Lean files with explicitly marked editable regions: EVOLVE-BLOCK regions contain proof code, while EVOLVE-VALUE regions allow the agent to determine values within the statement, including a conjecture’s truth value (Tsoukalas et al., 2026, Section 2 and Appendix A.2). We reconstruct our tasks from the statements and edit boundaries in APN’s public GitHub release,44 4 https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results removing the proofs and withholding truth values wherever these are marked editable. This preserves the fixed parts of each statement. We interpret these released specifications as corresponding to the tasks underlying APN’s reported comparison results, although the paper does not explicitly confirm the initial files used for those experiments.

We run these experiments in an isolated environment without internet access or access to existing solutions on the host filesystem. After observing attempts to use the Lean REPL to explore the filesystem, we also explicitly inform the model of this isolation to discourage such attempts and avoid wasting inference budget (Table 5). The reflection LLM also redirects the prover away from these attempts and toward mathematical work in the next iteration. This is part of the effective repair loop that supports h1’s efficiency (Section 4): carrying lessons from unproductive attempts into the next iteration helps direct additional inference budget toward sustained progress.

We follow Tsoukalas et al. (2026) in reporting inference cost conditional on success. This permits comparison with their published per-problem results. For kk parallel attempts, we sum all members’ costs up to the first accepted proof, including the costs of unsuccessful members. Groups with no accepted proof contribute to the failure rate but not to the conditional-cost mean. Thus this metric measures the token-based cost of successful searches; it does not measure total cost across successes and failures. APN does not report the failed-group costs needed for this comparison.

To measure how a larger inference budget improves success at fixed kk, we vary the same per-attempt dollar allowance $BB across problems. Within each group, attempts stop at the first accepted proof obtained within that allowance. For problem ii, let 𝒮i,k​(B)\mathcal{S}_{i,k}(B) be the successful kk-subsets of our n=16n=16 replicas under per-attempt allowance $BB. If τi,G\tau_{i,G} is the first eligible proof’s active-time timestamp and Ci,r​(τ)C_{i,r}(\tau) the recorded cumulative cost of replica rr, we compute

p^i,k​(B)=|𝒮i,k​(B)|(nk),c^i,k​(B)=∑G∈𝒮i,k​(B)∑r∈Gmin⁡{B,Ci,r​(τi,G)}|𝒮i,k​(B)|.\widehat{p}_{i,k}(B)=\frac{|\mathcal{S}_{i,k}(B)|}{\binom{n}{k}},\qquad\widehat{c}_{i,k}(B)=\frac{\sum_{G\in\mathcal{S}_{i,k}(B)}\sum_{r\in G}\min\{B,C_{i,r}(\tau_{i,G})\}}{|\mathcal{S}_{i,k}(B)|}. (1)

Active time excludes gaps between resumed sessions. Only completed model calls contribute cost, using the specified token prices. We average both coordinates equally over the same fixed problem set II:

c¯I,k​(B)=|I|−1​∑i∈Ic^i,k​(B),p¯I,k​(B)=|I|−1​∑i∈Ip^i,k​(B).\overline{c}_{I,k}(B)=|I|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}\widehat{c}_{i,k}(B),\qquad\overline{p}_{I,k}(B)=|I|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}\widehat{p}_{i,k}(B). (2)

The plotted frontier retains nondominated cost–success points, using only allowances for which every problem in II has an observed success and hence a defined conditional cost. APN basic’s pass@kk rates are its published grouped-run estimates; our rates use the subset estimator over recorded replicas. APN full reports ten attempts per problem. The published APN coordinates receive the same equal problem weights. This differs from pooling successful attempts, which would give easier problems more weight. The overlapping subsets do not provide independent observations for estimating uncertainty, and APN does not report uncertainty for this aggregate.

The cost–success frontier in Figure 1 compares the five problems with observed successes in all three systems: 12(i), 12(ii), 138, 152, and 26. This subset does not include Erdős 125: all h1 attempts encounter Lean timeouts, leaving its success-conditional cost undefined. Across the full six-problem set, including these failures, h1 achieves 68.75% at pass@1, close to APN full’s 71.67%, and surpasses APN full’s pass@1 success rate with 79.73% at pass@3 (Table 15).

Counting unsuccessful searches.

To compare compute allocation within h1, we also report mean spend over all groups, including those with no accepted proof. Let 𝒢i,k\mathcal{G}_{i,k} be all kk-subsets of the n=16n=16 replicas, and let Ci,r​(∞)C_{i,r}(\infty) denote a replica’s recorded terminal cost. The unconditional estimate is

u^i,k​(B)=1(nk)​[∑G∈𝒮i,k​(B)∑r∈Gmin⁡{B,Ci,r​(τi,G)}+∑G∈𝒢i,k∖𝒮i,k​(B)∑r∈Gmin⁡{B,Ci,r​(∞)}].\widehat{u}_{i,k}(B)=\frac{1}{\binom{n}{k}}\left[\sum_{G\in\mathcal{S}_{i,k}(B)}\sum_{r\in G}\min\{B,C_{i,r}(\tau_{i,G})\}+\sum_{G\in\mathcal{G}_{i,k}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{i,k}(B)}\sum_{r\in G}\min\{B,C_{i,r}(\infty)\}\right]. (3)

We use the same recorded attempts, token prices, dollar caps, and first-proof cancellation rule as in Equation 1; only the averaging includes unsuccessful groups. Each problem receives equal weight. Conditioning on success selects different groups as kk changes, so the conditional metric alone does not describe the full spending trade-off. It does not mathematically prevent repetition from dominating a pass@1 operating point: a quick proof in one replica can cancel expensive searches in the others. We omit APN from the unconditional plots because its failed-group costs are unavailable.

For a hypothetical example, suppose independent attempts spend at the same constant rate and solve at $1 with probability 0.80.8, solve at $100 with probability 0.10.1, or fail at $100 with probability 0.10.1. Pass@1 succeeds with probability 0.90.9 at conditional mean cost (0.8×1+0.1×100)/0.9=$12(0.8\times 1+0.1\times 100)/0.9=\$12. Two parallel attempts, cancelled at the first proof, succeed with probability 0.990.99 at conditional mean cost (0.96×2+0.03×200)/0.99=$8(0.96\times 2+0.03\times 200)/0.99=\$8: a quick success occurs with probability 0.960.96, and a success without a quick one with probability 0.030.03. This establishes dominance of one operating point, not of the entire pass@1 curve.

Figure 14 compares using a common dollar allowance with using a common active-time allowance across problems. Both give the same final costs and success rates, but different intermediate curves.

E.7 Model choice at different budgets

E.8 Additional comparisons with AxProverBase and analysis of failed attempts

With Gemini 3 Flash on the PutnamBench subset, h1 solves all 18 problems solved by AxProverBase and 51 additional problems. On those 51, mean proposer-call counts are 287 for AxProverBase and 275 for h1. Mean output per problem, including reflection, is 5.97M versus 0.628M tokens; mean input is 4.24M versus 23.13M, respectively. The fraction of input served from cache is 0.04% for AxProverBase and 78.8% for h1. AxProverBase regenerates a complete candidate after feedback; h1 retains the file and makes local edits. These observations connect the token-cost difference to how the systems preserve work, without isolating it from their other design differences.

For example, on putnam_1972_b4, AxProverBase uses tokens equivalent to $20.01 over 287 builds, including 175 bad-import and 84 syntax failures. h1 solves it at an API-equivalent cost of $0.15 with 20 local edits, three REPL tests, and one submission. Across the 51 h1-only solves, AxProverBase performs 13,446 reflections and h1 performs 316, while the systems differ in whether they regenerate or edit the working file.

E.9 Additional comparisons with Claude Code and analysis of failed attempts

With the same Claude model, native Claude Code (with its built-in shell and file tools), Claude Code with our prompt and Lean tools through MCP (which replace the built-in tools), and h1 solve 81/95/99 PutnamBench subset problems and 63/73/83 FATE-X problems, respectively (Figures 5 and , right). The tools expose Lean feedback and SafeVerify rejection within the session; h1 additionally enforces validation and another repair round after rejection.

Relative to native Claude Code, exposing final-proof validation addresses a frequent failure mode. Of 30 problems solved by h1 where native Claude Code stops normally without an accepted proof, 28 end with an artifact rejected by SafeVerify. Adding our Lean tools to Claude Code solves 20 of these problems. h1 uses multiple rounds on 21 of the 30.

Relative to Claude Code with MCP tools, h1 additionally controls how execution continues after failures. On FATE-X problem 19, Claude Code with our tools resubmits an unchanged file 170 times, whereas h1 edits after each of 17 negative outcomes and succeeds.

The MCP integration also leaves API-call retries under Claude Code’s control. Some Claude Code runs fail through API-call errors and repeated timeouts. We took care to give these baselines their strongest showing: we restarted affected runs from scratch, and reran configurations whose wall-time limit was binding with a larger allowance. Exposing Lean tools through MCP does not give the experimenter the same control over Claude Code’s internal retries and failure handling as implementing the harness directly. In h1, these policies are explicit: transient connection failures can retry the same call, while verifier failures return feedback for further edits.

E.10 Model and benchmark release dates

Appendix F Tool, Prompt, and Reflection Ablations

The reflection-input ablation varies the context supplied to the reflection LLM, independently of its system prompt. With the transcript, it receives the latest attempt’s reasoning, final code, verifier feedback, and interaction transcript. The distilled final attempt consists of the multi-turn LLM’s account of its latest attempt, the final Lean code, the verifier feedback, and the previous reflection summary; the sequence of intermediate model turns, tool calls, and tool results is omitted.

Removing the transcript reduces input costs for reflection by 95% on the PutnamBench subset and 90% on FATE-X, but prover-call costs rise by 9.6% and 7.3%, respectively (Table 16). The increase occurs on 64/100 and 74/100 problems. Mean prover-call counts rise by 12.1% [1.4, 23.5] and 18.3% [11.1, 26.2]. Total-cost changes remain small; intervals span zero and reflect variation across paired problems.
